findings.problem: unwrap() on Result from parse::<u32>() is a panic path. Any malformed line (non-numeric text, negative numbers, overflow) causes a panic at runtime. This is a forbidden construct in production-reachable code.
findings.failure_mode: Denial of service: a single non-numeric line in the input crashes the entire function. Untrusted or streaming input will reliably trigger this panic.
findings.fix: Return a typed error: fn parse_scores(input: &str) -> Result<Vec<u32>, ParseError>. Replace .unwrap() with proper Result propagation or an explicit error enum that distinguishes parse failures from input issues.

findings.problem: Unbounded collect: lines() iterates over all input with no fixed upper bound or capacity hint. The function accepts arbitrary-length input and allocates an unbounded Vec. No max input size, no try_reserve, no bounded collection type.
findings.failure_mode: Out-of-memory on untrusted or streaming input. An attacker or misconfigured consumer can supply input that exceeds available memory. No graceful failure path exists.
findings.fix: Declare a maximum input size or line count. Use try_reserve before collecting, or return a resource error when input exceeds the bound. Consider a bounded output type like ArrayVec or a streaming iterator that yields results incrementally.

findings.problem: Result from parse::<u32>() is ignored via unwrap(). Power of Ten Rule 7 requires callers check non-void returns and callees check parameter validity. This function silently panics on bad input instead of returning a typed error.
findings.failure_mode: Silent data loss: partial results are discarded on the first parse failure. The caller has no way to know which line failed or how many scores were successfully parsed before the crash.
findings.fix: Change the return type to Result<Vec<u32>, ParseScoreError> and propagate parse errors with context (line number, raw string). Validate input parameters at the boundary.

findings.problem: Hot or untrusted-input path grows memory with no max size declaration, no checked capacity arithmetic, no try_reserve call, and no typed resource error. Vec::new() followed by unbounded push is exactly the pattern rejected by the storage placement and allocation discipline rules.
findings.failure_mode: Uncontrolled heap growth on adversarial or high-volume input. No allocation budget or regression guard exists.
findings.fix: Add a max_input_lines or max_total_score count parameter. Call try_reserve with the declared maximum. Return a resource error (e.g., ResourceError::ExceededBudget) when the bound is exceeded instead of allocating unboundedly.

findings.problem: No benchmark target exists. No dev-dependencies for criterion or iai-callgrind. No bench section in Cargo.toml. Performance claims cannot be made without benchmark evidence, and the function has no measurable performance characteristics documented.
findings.failure_mode: Any performance optimization or claim is ungrounded. Cannot verify that changes improve or degrade latency, throughput, or allocation behavior.
findings.fix: Add a [[bench]] section with a criterion benchmark that measures parse_latency and parse_throughput across input sizes. Add criterion as a dev-dependency. Document baseline numbers before any optimization.

findings.problem: No rust-toolchain.toml present. No pinned nightly toolchain for deterministic builds. No clippy configuration, no deny directives, no fmt configuration. Static analysis gates cannot be verified.
findings.failure_mode: Build behavior varies across toolchain versions. No reproducible CI gate. Lint and analysis findings may be silently missed.
findings.fix: Add a rust-toolchain.toml with a pinned dated nightly, minimal profile, and rustfmt/clippy/rust-src/llvm-tools-preview components. Add [lints] section with deny directives for unsafe_code, unwrap_used, expect_used, and panic in result_fn.

findings.problem: The function parses human-readable text at runtime on every call with no precompilation, no numeric IDs, no dense IR, and no caching. If this function is called repeatedly with the same or similar input format, it repeatedly re-parses what could be a compiled constant or prevalidated artifact.
findings.failure_mode: Redundant runtime work: every call re-parses the entire input string even when the format is known at compile time. No prevalidated artifact exists for the repeated-evaluation case.
findings.fix: If the score format is stable, compile a prevalidated format descriptor at build time (e.g., a macros-generated parser or compile-time validated schema). For repeated evaluation of the same input, cache the compiled result keyed by content hash.

findings.problem: Function returns Vec<u32> forcing heap allocation on every call. No caller-owned output buffer option, no preallocated capacity, no with_capacity hint. Every invocation allocates a new heap buffer.
findings.failure_mode: Heap allocation per call. No buffer reuse. Allocators contend on every invocation. Tail latency impacted by allocation cost.
findings.fix: Provide a second API: fn parse_scores_into(input: &str, out: &mut Vec<u32>) -> Result<(), ParseError> that reuses a caller-provided buffer. Add fn parse_scores_with_capacity(input: &str, capacity: usize) -> Result<Vec<u32>, ParseError> that calls try_reserve.

findings.problem: Function is 6 lines including the signature, but the entire body is a single chained iterator with no invariant exposure. The function does not expose any invariants through types or constructors - it silently panics on bad input.
findings.failure_mode: No clear failure boundary. The single chained expression hides the fact that any stage of the pipeline can fail.
findings.fix: Split into a validated constructor or a function with explicit error handling. Even at 6 lines, the function should return a Result to expose the failure invariant.

findings.problem: Iterator chain (lines -> map -> collect) hides the control flow. Each stage can fail: lines() produces strings, trim() produces &str, parse() produces Result. The chain conflates all three operations into a single expression with no intermediate error handling.
findings.failure_mode: Caller receives no information about which stage produced a failure. No partial results are recoverable. The failure mode is binary (success or panic) with no diagnostic detail.
findings.fix: Use an explicit loop with line-by-line error handling that reports the line number and raw content on parse failure. Separate validation from transformation.

findings.problem: No assembly/IR evidence exists for the parse chain. No proof that LLVM can optimize the iterator chain to efficient bounds-checked loops. No evidence that the generated code avoids redundant string allocation per line.
findings.failure_mode: Hidden allocation per line: if LLVM cannot prove the line buffer reuse, each iteration may allocate a String. This is not visible from source alone.
findings.fix: Run cargo asm on the compiled function to verify the iterator chain compiles to efficient bounds-checked code. Check for per-line String allocations.

findings.problem: No second-ring tooling configured. No cargo-auditable, no SBOM generation, no cargo-semver-checks baseline. No safety or API compatibility verification infrastructure.
findings.failure_mode: Undetected dependency issues, API regressions, and missing provenance for the crate.
findings.fix: Add cargo-auditable as a build dependency for provenance. Configure cargo-semver-checks with a baseline revision for public API stability.

no rust-toolchain.toml - no pinned nightly for reproducible builds

no assembly/IR evidence - no proof the iterator chain compiles to efficient code
no profiler data - no allocation profiling to confirm per-call heap churn

residual_risk: The crate has multiple BLOCKER violations that make it unsuitable for production use: panic-on-malformed-input via unwrap(), unbounded memory allocation with no input validation, no error types, no benchmarks, and no toolchain pinning. Even if these were fixed, no formal verification, assembly evidence, or behavior tests exist to prove the corrected implementation meets safety or performance requirements. The fundamental parsing logic is trivial, so the fix surface is small, but the absence of any testing or measurement infrastructure means zero assurance that corrected code actually works correctly under hostile input.
